text: A small greyscale photo is a grid of numbers, one per pixel, and a colour photo is three such grids. We could flatten that grid into one long vector and feed it to the layers we have built, but every neuron would then need a separate weight for every pixel, and a pattern it learned in one corner would mean nothing to it in another. Images deserve a layer that understands that a pattern is the same pattern wherever it appears.

That layer is the convolution. It uses a small grid of weights, typically three by three, called a kernel or filter. We lay the kernel over a patch of the image, multiply each weight by the pixel beneath it and add everything up, which is simply a dot product between the kernel and the patch. Then we slide the kernel one pixel along and do it again, like a magnifying glass sweeping across a page, and the numbers it produces form a new grid called a feature map.

What the kernel detects depends on its weights. Put negative weights in its left column and positive weights in its right, and it compares the brightness on the two sides of each position. Over a flat region the two sides cancel and the output is zero, but where the image changes from dark to bright, the response is strong, so the feature map lights up along vertical edges and stays dark everywhere else.

Because the same nine weights are used at every position, the layer finds its pattern anywhere in the image, and if the object moves, its response moves with it. This weight sharing also makes convolution remarkably economical: the kernel has nine weights whether the image is tiny or enormous, whereas a fully connected layer needs a weight for every pixel.

Sliding a three by three kernel across a six by six image fits only four positions in each direction, so the feature map shrinks to four by four. In general, the output size is the input size minus the kernel size, plus one. Padding the image with a border of zeros keeps the size unchanged, and a stride greater than one makes the kernel jump several pixels at a time, shrinking the map on purpose.

In practice we do not design kernels by hand. A convolutional layer holds many kernels, each producing its own feature map, called a channel, and their weights are learned by backpropagation like any others, so the network discovers for itself which patterns are worth detecting. Strictly speaking, deep learning libraries compute cross-correlation, since they do not flip the kernel as mathematicians do, but everyone calls it convolution.

Language models rarely use convolutions, yet they rely on the same principle of sharing weights across positions, applying one feed-forward network to every token. Vision transformers even begin by cutting an image into patches with a strided convolution. Next we see how pooling summarises feature maps, and how stacked layers build a hierarchy of features.
